catalog_quote: The transcription in this book indicates stress only on short vowels, since stress on long vowels is predictable. Most words only have one long vowel or diphthong, in which case the stress falls on the long vowel or diphthong. If a word has more than one long vowel, then the long vowel nearest the end is stressed. As discussed in §2.2, unstressed long vowels are the result of a lost consonant or contraction of ǝy or ǝw. Stressed short vowels occur mainly in non-final closed syllables and final CVCC syllables. Most exceptions to this rule are the result of lost consonants, e.g., nákak (< underlying *nákʿǝk < *nōkʿǝk). new_statements.rule_in_words: Quantity-sensitive, right-oriented: stress goes to the (rightmost) long vowel or diphthong — equivalently (Watson & al-Mahri 2018) to a final superheavy syllable (CVV#, CVVC#, CVCC#), otherwise to the rightmost non-final heavy syllable (CVV or CVC; final C extrametrical), otherwise to the leftmost CV syllable of the stem. Long vowels surface only under stress, so vowel length and stress largely co-diagnose each other.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Rubin says nothing. Watson & al-Mahri 2018 sec. 4.3 and Watson et al. 2024 fn. 6: secondary stress on heavy syllables / heads of bimoraic trochaic feet to the left of the primary stress (ˌūbaˈnīt 'white f.s.', ˌraḥbɛ̄ˈnōt 'little town', ˌbīˈrōk 'knees').
new_statements.exceptions: Rubin: apparent short stressed vowels in open syllables come from lost ʿ/ʾ (nákak < *nákʿǝk); a few exceptional words (mǝn 'from', bǝr 'son of', bɛr 'already'); in verb paradigms stress stays fixed unless a long-vowel suffix is added; possessive suffixes unstressed unless noun ends in stressed vowel. Watson & al-Mahri 2018: lexical final stress on -ah/-eh/-oh/-uh/-ɛʔ (final-weak verbs bˈkuh, adverbs īˈmoh, ṯruh/ḥruh, familial diminutives, dual subject markers); 3ms suffix -ih/-ah always stressed; word-level (most pronoun) suffixes invisible to stress; epenthetic vowels never stressed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement for citation/word forms of Omani (Dhofari) Mehri. Watson & al-Mahri 2018 argue the stress domain is the stem plus stem-level suffixes (word-level suffixes adjoined, unstressable) and note phrase-level clash-driven retraction (ˈḏīma ˌbahˈlīt vs aˈbahˌlīt ˈḏīmah).
new_statements.identity_note: Rubin 2018 describes Omani (Dhofari) Mehri, chiefly the eastern Dhofar variety of Johnstone's consultant Ali Musallam; Watson & al-Mahri 2018 and Watson et al. 2024 describe Central Dhofari Mehri of the Bit Thuwar tribe (they reject the label 'Omani Mehri'). Yemeni Mehri (Mahriyōt of Qishn / al-Ghaydah, Sharqiyah) is not covered by the quoted statement; Simeone-Senelle 1997 (p. 386) states the same 'last long syllable, else first syllable' rule for Mehri generally. All fall under language-level glottocode mehr1241; no dialect glottocodes asserted here.

sources.note: Sec. 2.3 'Word Stress', p. 50: stress falls on the long vowel/diphthong; if more than one long vowel, the one nearest the end is stressed; stressed short vowels occur mainly in non-final closed syllables and final CVCC; a few lexical exceptions (mǝn, bǝr, bɛr); in verb paradigms stress stays fixed unless a long-vowel suffix is added. Sec. 2.2 (p. 41-42): long vowels occur only in open stressed syllables or final stressed -CVC; transcription marks stress only on short vowels (p. 17).

sources.note: Fn. 6 (advance-article p. 6): 'Feet in Mehri are bimoraic trochees. Primary word stress is assigned to a final superheavy syllable, otherwise to the right-most heavy (CVV or CVC) syllable of the word stem, or to a word-final dual suffix or final weak verb ending, with secondary stress assigned to heavy syllables to the left of the primary stressed syllable.. In the absence of a heavy syllable or stressable suffix in the word, stress is assigned to the left-most CV syllable of the word stem, as in yəgáwər, láhina.' sources.note: Dedicated study. Sec. 3-3.1 (AM pp. 6-8): 'Mehri generally assigns word stress according to syllable weight in basic stems, and.. exhibits lexical stress in a few cases.' Algorithm (1): a. monosyllables CvCC/(C)CvvC/Cvv stressed; b. multisyllables: stress final Cvv, CvvC or CvCC (bīˈrōk, aˈtēm); c. otherwise the rightmost non-final heavy syllable Cvv/CvC (ˈśēḥaz, ˈnūka, yiˈġōrab); d. otherwise the left-most Cv syllable of the stem (yiˈgawar, ˈlahina).
